simple: how fast one quantity changes when another one changes.
analogy: how many metres the cart gains per clap.
precise: for a quantity x that depends on t, the change in x divided by the change in t; its unit is the unit of x divided by the unit of t (m/s for position over time).
source: D1 of F0-64 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the change over a whole stretch of time, divided by the length of that stretch.
analogy: the gap between two sticky notes divided by the time between the claps.
precise: (x(t + h) − x(t)) / h for a step h ≠ 0; geometrically the slope of the secant line through the two points of the graph.
source: D1 of F0-64 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B2 of F0-64 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the value an answer gets closer and closer to as you make a step smaller and smaller.
analogy: the number the clap-by-clap speeds settle towards when the claps come faster and faster.
precise: L is the limit of g(h) as h → 0 if g(h) can be made as close to L as you like by taking h close enough to 0 (h ≠ 0).
source: B2 of F0-64 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the rate of change at one instant.
analogy: the cart's speed at the exact moment of one clap.
precise: x′(t) = dx/dt = limh→0 (x(t + h) − x(t)) / h, when this limit exists; the slope of the tangent line to the graph at t.
source: B2 of F0-64 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen); D1 of F0-64 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the straight line that just touches a curve at one point and points the way the curve is heading there.
analogy: the direction the cart would keep going if nothing changed its speed from that moment on.
precise: the line y = x(t₀) + x′(t₀)(t − t₀); the best straight-line approximation of the curve near t₀.
source: B2 of F0-64 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: speed with a direction (a sign).
analogy: how fast the cart rolls, counted negative when it rolls back towards the start.
precise: v(t) = x′(t), the derivative of position with respect to time, in m/s for straight-line motion.
source: B1 of F0-64 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); D1 of F0-64 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how fast the velocity changes.
analogy: how much faster the cart gets from one clap to the next.
precise: a(t) = v′(t) = x″(t), the second derivative of position, in m/s².
source: B1 of F0-64 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); D1 of F0-64 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: short-cuts that give a derivative without computing a limit each time.
analogy: a recipe card that turns a formula for position straight into a formula for speed.
precise: the power, sum, constant-multiple, product, quotient and chain rules, together with the derivatives of e^t, sin t and cos t; each follows from the limit definition.
source: B2 of F0-64 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: pretending a curve is a straight line for a short moment.
analogy: guessing where the cart will be a moment later from where it is and how fast it goes now.
precise: x(t + h) ≈ x(t) + x′(t)·h, with an error that shrinks like h² when x has a second derivative (the first terms of Taylor's formula).
source: B2 of F0-64 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the total amount that builds up when something flows in at a known rate.
analogy: the water collected in the bath.
precise: the quantity Q(T) = Q(0) + ∫₀ to T q(t) dt obtained from a rate q(t); its unit is the unit of the rate times the unit of time.
source: D1 of F0-65 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an estimate of a total made by adding up thin rectangles.
analogy: Kofi's list of "flow this minute × one minute", added up.
precise: Σk f(tk*)·Δtk over a partition of [a, b] into pieces of width Δtk, with tk* a point in each piece (left end, right end or midpoint).
source: B2 of F0-65 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the exact total, the value the sums settle towards as the pieces get thinner.
analogy: the true amount of water, which Kofi's lists approach as he reads the gauge more often.
precise: ∫a^b f(t) dt = the limit of the Riemann sums as the widest piece shrinks to zero, when that limit exists; geometrically the signed area between the graph and the t-axis.
source: B2 of F0-65 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the function being added up.
analogy: the flow gauge reading.
precise: f in ∫ f(t) dt.
source: B2 of F0-65 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a function whose derivative is the one you started with.
analogy: the bath's water-level formula, whose rate of change is the tap's flow.
precise: F is an antiderivative of f if F′ = f; any two differ by a constant, written ∫ f(t) dt = F(t) + C (the indefinite integral).
source: B2 of F0-65 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the rule that adding up a rate gives the change in the amount.
analogy: the water added equals the final level minus the starting level, however the tap was turned.
precise: if f is continuous on [a, b] and F′ = f, then ∫a^b f(t) dt = F(b) − F(a); and d/dt ∫a^t f(s) ds = f(t).
source: B2 of F0-65 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: adding up thin slanted strips instead of flat-topped rectangles.
analogy: using the average of the gauge readings at the start and end of each minute.
precise: ∫ ≈ Σk ½(f(tk) + f(tk+1))·Δt; for a function with a continuous second derivative its error shrinks like Δt².
source: B2 of F0-65 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen); R1 of F0-65 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: working out where you are only from how fast you went and for how long.
analogy: guessing the bath level only from the gauge, never looking at the water.
precise: estimating position by integrating measured velocity (or acceleration twice) from a known start, without an external position measurement; errors in the rate accumulate.
source: B1 of F0-65 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); D1 of F0-65 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the steady rate that would give the same total.
analogy: the one tap setting that would fill the bath equally in the same time.
source: B2 of F0-65 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the time between two readings.
analogy: Mei reads the ruler every two seconds.
precise: the interval between successive samples x[k] = x(kΔt) of a signal; its inverse is the sample rate.
source: D1 of F0-66 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a derivative estimated from two or more nearby samples.
analogy: the change between two ruler readings divided by the time between them.
precise: forward (x[k+1] − x[k])/Δt, backward (x[k] − x[k−1])/Δt, central (x[k+1] − x[k−1])/(2Δt); errors of order Δt, Δt and Δt² for smooth signals.
source: B2 of F0-66 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen); R1 of F0-66 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the error a formula makes even with perfect numbers, because it uses a finite step.
analogy: the difference between "speed over 2 s" and "speed right now" when the tap is being turned.
precise: the part of the error that comes from cutting off Taylor's series; for the forward difference ½·x″·Δt.
source: B2 of F0-66 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: rounding a reading to the nearest step the sensor can show.
analogy: the ruler that only has centimetre marks.
precise: replacing a value x by q·round(x/q) for a step q, an error of at most q/2; for an encoder q is one count, 2π/(counts per revolution) radians.
source: U2 of F0-66 (university chapters cited for what they teach); D1 of F0-66 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: small wobbles in readings become big wobbles in the speed you compute from them.
analogy: a one-centimetre wobble over two seconds looks like a fast fill.
precise: a sample error of size ε produces an error up to 2ε/Δt in a two-point difference; the shorter Δt, the larger.
source: D1 of F0-66 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R2 of F0-66 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a running guess that moves part of the way towards each new reading.
analogy: Kofi's calm guess of the filling speed.
precise: y[k] = y[k−1] + α·(x[k] − y[k−1]) with α = Δt/(τ + Δt), the backward-Euler form of τ·y′ + y = x; HW302 calls the same update an exponential moving average.
source: D1 of F0-66 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); B1 of F0-66 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how late the calm value is compared with the real one.
analogy: the calm guess notices the tap opening a few seconds late.
precise: for slowly changing inputs, a first-order low-pass filter's output trails its input by about τ; a difference over a window of length W trails by about W/2.
source: B1 of F0-66 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); D1 of F0-66 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a total to which you add "value × Δt" at every sample.
analogy: Kofi's list of flow readings added up.
precise: S[k] = S[k−1] + x[k]·Δt, the rectangle rule of F0-65 updated one sample at a time.
source: D1 of F0-66 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a rule that computes a command from the error now, the sum of past errors, and how fast the error changes.
analogy: adjusting the tap from how far the bath is from full, how long it has been short, and how fast it is filling.
precise: u[k] = Kp·e[k] + Ki·S[k] + Kd·D[k], with S a running sum and D a (filtered) difference of the error or of the measurement (RB202 F9-21).
source: B1 of F0-66 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a rule that says how fast something changes, in terms of what it is now.
analogy: "the trolley speeds up less the faster it already rolls".
precise: an equation relating an unknown function to its derivatives; an ordinary differential equation (ODE) has one independent variable, here time t.
source: B2 of F0-67 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen); B1 of F0-67 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the highest derivative that appears.
analogy: whether the rule talks about speed only, or also about how the speed changes.
precise: m·v′ = F − c·v is first order in v; written for position, m·x″ + c·x′ = F, it is second order in x.
source: B2 of F0-67 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: where things start.
analogy: the trolley standing still before Lucía pushes.
precise: the values of the unknown (and, for order n, its first n − 1 derivatives) at the starting time, for example v(0) = 0; with them, a well-behaved ODE has exactly one solution.
source: B2 of F0-67 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: drag that grows in proportion to speed.
analogy: the carpet holding the wheels back harder the faster they roll.
precise: a force −c·v opposing the velocity, with coefficient c in N·s/m; a linear model, accurate for some systems over limited speed ranges.
source: B1 of F0-67 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a drag of fixed size whenever something slides or rolls, whatever the speed.
analogy: the steady resistance of the trolley's stiff wheel.
precise: a force of magnitude Fc opposing the direction of motion, −Fc·sign(v) for v ≠ 0; at v = 0 the friction force is whatever is needed, up to a static limit, to keep the body at rest.
source: B1 of F0-67 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the speed at which the push and the drag balance, so the speed stops changing.
analogy: the steady rolling speed of the trolley under a steady push.
precise: an equilibrium of v′ = f(v), a value with f(v*) = 0; for m·v′ = F − c·v it is v* = F/c.
source: D1 of F0-67 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: closing the same fraction of the remaining gap in every equal stretch of time.
analogy: the trolley closes most of the gap to its steady speed quickly, then ever more slowly.
precise: the solution v(t) = v* + (v(0) − v*)·e^−t/τ of the linear first-order ODE τ·v′ + v = v*; after τ, 63.2 % of the gap is closed, after 3τ 95.0 %, after 5τ 99.3 %.
source: D1 of F0-67 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R4 of F0-67 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: moving the state forward by a small time using the current rates.
analogy: "at this speed, in the next millisecond the trolley moves this far and speeds up this much".
precise: x ← x + Δt·f(x, u), the linear approximation of F0-64 applied repeatedly; its error over a fixed time span shrinks in proportion to Δt (explicit Euler method, studied in MA302 F0-76).
source: B2 of F0-67 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen); R1 of F0-67 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the few numbers that, together with the inputs, decide everything that happens next.
analogy: the trolley's position and speed right now.
precise: a set of variables whose present values and the future inputs determine the future solution; for the cart, (x, v).
source: B1 of F0-67 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: what a system does when its input is switched from zero to a fixed value and held.
analogy: the kettle switched on; the flour dropped on the scale.
precise: the output y(t), from rest, for the input u(t) = 0 for t < 0 and u(t) = U for t ≥ 0; often normalised to U = 1 (unit step).
source: B1 of F0-68 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a system that approaches its final value smoothly, without overshoot, closing the same fraction of the gap in each equal time.
analogy: the kettle warming up.
precise: τ·y′ + y = K·u; unit step response y = K(1 − e^−t/τ).
source: B1 of F0-68 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); D1 of F0-68 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much output you finally get per unit of steady input.
analogy: how many degrees hotter per unit of heater setting, once everything has settled.
precise: K = lim y(t)/U for a step of size U in a stable system; for a motor's speed, rad/s per volt.
source: B1 of F0-68 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a system with two stores of energy that can swing past its final value.
analogy: the scale's spring and moving platform.
precise: y″ + 2ζωn·y′ + ωn²·y = K·ωn²·u, for example a mass–spring–damper m·x″ + c·x′ + k·x = F.
source: B1 of F0-68 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how fast the system would swing if nothing slowed it down.
analogy: the needle's bouncing speed with no friction.
precise: ωn = √(k/m) for a mass–spring, in rad/s; the undamped oscillation frequency.
source: B1 of F0-68 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a single number saying how strongly the swinging is slowed down.
analogy: how sticky the scale's mechanism is: a little, and it wobbles a lot; a lot, and it creeps to the value.
precise: ζ = c/(2√(k·m)) for a mass–spring–damper; under-damped 0 < ζ < 1 (overshoots), critically damped ζ = 1, over-damped ζ > 1.
source: B1 of F0-68 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how far the output goes past its final value, as a percentage.
analogy: how far past the true weight the needle swings first.
precise: Mp = (ymax − y∞)/y∞; for the standard second-order system Mp = exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)).
source: B1 of F0-68 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); R2 of F0-68 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: when the first, biggest overshoot happens, and how fast the wobbles really are.
analogy: when the needle is furthest past the mark.
precise: ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²) and tp = π/ωd, half a period of the damped oscillation.
source: B1 of F0-68 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long until the output stays close to its final value for good.
analogy: how long before you can read the scale.
precise: the last time the response is outside a band (here ±2 %) around y∞; the estimate 4/(ζωn) holds for moderately under-damped systems only.
source: B1 of F0-68 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); R2 of F0-68 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much each wobble shrinks compared with the one before.
analogy: the second swing of the needle past the mark compared with the first.
precise: δ = ln(a₁/a₂) for two successive overshoots a₁, a₂ one period apart; ζ = δ/√(4π² + δ²).
source: B1 of F0-68 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); D1 of F0-68 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a fixed recipe that turns a function of time into a function of a new variable s.
analogy: converting cups into grams with the fridge table.
precise: F(s) = ℒ{f}(s) = ∫₀∞ f(t)·e^−st dt, defined for the values of s where the integral converges.
source: B1 of F0-69 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); B2 of F0-69 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the variable of the transformed world; it can be a real or a complex number.
analogy: the unit "grams" in Ravi's conversion.
precise: s = σ + jω with unit 1/s; e^−st is a decaying or growing oscillation, so F(s) measures how much f contains of each such pattern.
source: B1 of F0-69 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a function of time and its transform, listed together.
analogy: one line of the conversion table: "1 cup of flour = 120 g".
precise: f(t) ↔ F(s), for example 1 ↔ 1/s, e^−at ↔ 1/(s + a); the inverse transform of F is the f it came from (unique for the functions used in this course).
source: B1 of F0-69 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); R1 of F0-69 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: differentiating in time becomes multiplying by s, minus the starting value.
analogy: a step that is fiddly in cups but a single multiplication in grams.
precise: ℒ{f′} = sF(s) − f(0); ℒ{f″} = s²F(s) − s·f(0) − f′(0); and ℒ{∫₀ to t f} = F(s)/s.
source: B1 of F0-69 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); D1 of F0-69 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: splitting one complicated fraction into a sum of simple ones that are in the table.
analogy: splitting a big shopping total back into the items that made it.
precise: writing a proper rational function N(s)/D(s) with distinct roots pk of D as Σ Ak/(s − pk), with Ak = [(s − pk)·N/D] evaluated at s = pk (the cover-up rule).
source: B2 of F0-69 (the calculus textbook to be chosen by the Dean — not yet chosen) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a value of s where the transform's formula blows up.
analogy: a line of the table that marks a strong ingredient: it decides the taste of the whole dish.
precise: a root of the denominator of a rational F(s); each pole p contributes a term e^pt to f(t). F0-71 builds stability on this.
source: B1 of F0-69 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a shortcut that gives where a signal ends up, without solving for all of it.
analogy: reading the final weight off the converted totals without converting every step back.
precise: limt→∞ f(t) = lims→0 s·F(s), valid only if f(t) has a limit, which is guaranteed when every pole of s·F(s) has a negative real part.
source: B1 of F0-69 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); R3 of F0-69 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a shortcut for where a signal starts just after t = 0.
analogy: the first ingredient on the converted list.
precise: f(0⁺) = lims→∞ s·F(s), when the limit exists.
source: B1 of F0-69 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a formula in s that says how a system turns its input into its output.
analogy: the rule "one quarter turn of the tap gives three degrees warmer, after a while".
precise: for a linear time-invariant system at rest, G(s) = Y(s)/U(s), the ratio of the Laplace transforms of output and input with all initial conditions zero; for an ODE it is a ratio of polynomials.
source: B1 of F0-70 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a drawing of a system as boxes (each with a transfer function) joined by arrows that carry signals.
analogy: a sketch of the shower: tap, pipe, skin, brain, joined by arrows.
precise: a directed graph whose edges are signals and whose nodes are blocks (multiply by G(s)), summing junctions (add or subtract signals) and branch points (copy a signal).
source: B1 of F0-70 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the thing being controlled.
analogy: the pipes and the water heater.
precise: the part of a control system whose output is to be regulated, including the actuator when it is not modelled separately; written G(s) or P(s).
source: B1 of F0-70 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: what you get going once round the loop with the loop cut open.
analogy: how much warmer the water gets per degree of "too cold" felt, if you turned the tap once and did not check again.
precise: L(s) = C(s)·G(s)·H(s), the product of all blocks round the loop; L(0) is the loop gain at DC.
source: B1 of F0-70 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); D1 of F0-70 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how the whole loop, with feedback working, turns the setpoint into the output.
analogy: how the shower temperature follows what Mira wants.
precise: with negative feedback, T(s) = C(s)G(s)/(1 + C(s)G(s)H(s)); its denominator 1 + L(s) decides the loop's dynamics.
source: B1 of F0-70 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); R1 of F0-70 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the difference between setpoint and output that is left once everything has settled.
analogy: the shower ending up a little cooler than wanted, because Mira only turns the tap in proportion to how cold she feels.
precise: e(∞) = limt→∞(r − y); for a step r and a stable loop, e(∞) = r/(1 + L(0)) when H = 1 (final value theorem, F0-69).
source: D1 of F0-70 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R2 of F0-70 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: feedback that pushes the output further in the direction it is already going.
analogy: the back-to-front tap.
precise: a loop whose summing junction adds the fed-back signal (or, equivalently, whose loop gain has the wrong sign), giving T = CG/(1 − CGH); with enough gain it moves a pole into the right half-plane.
source: B1 of F0-70 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); R3 of F0-70 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the actuator cannot deliver more than its limit, however hard the controller asks.
analogy: the tap turned hard against its stop.
precise: a nonlinearity u = clamp(v, umin, umax) between controller and plant; while it is active, the loop is effectively open and the linear transfer-function analysis does not apply.
source: B1 of F0-70 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); R3 of F0-70 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a system is stable if, after a disturbance, it settles down again instead of drifting or growing.
analogy: the karaoke loop at a low volume: a clap dies away.
precise: a linear time-invariant system is asymptotically stable if every solution of its unforced equation decays to zero; equivalently, every pole of its transfer function has a negative real part (lies in the open left half of the s-plane).
source: B1 of F0-71 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of the s-plane to the left of the vertical axis, where the real part of s is negative.
analogy: the "volume low enough" side of the knob.
precise: {s : Re(s) < 0}; a pole p there gives a term e^pt that decays.
source: D1 of F0-71 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the polynomial whose roots are the closed-loop poles.
analogy: the recipe that decides whether the loop howls.
precise: for a loop with L(s) = N(s)/D(s), the denominator of 1 + L(s), that is D(s) + N(s); first met in F0-68.
source: B1 of F0-71 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); D1 of F0-71 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a test that tells you whether all roots of a polynomial are in the left half-plane, without finding them.
analogy: a rule printed on the karaoke box: "keep volume × room echo below this number".
precise: a polynomial with real coefficients has all roots in the open left half-plane exactly when every entry of the first column of its Routh array is positive; for a3s³ + a2s² + a1s + a0 with all ai > 0 this reduces to a2a1 > a3a0.
source: B1 of F0-71 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); R4 of F0-71 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the gain at which the loop is exactly on the edge between settling and growing.
analogy: the volume setting where the howl just starts.
precise: the smallest gain K for which a closed-loop pole reaches the imaginary axis; at that gain the loop oscillates steadily at the frequency of the crossing.
source: D1 of F0-71 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs); R1 of F0-71 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many times the gain could be raised before the loop becomes unstable.
analogy: how many more notches of volume are left before the howl.
precise: the ratio of the critical gain to the gain in use (often given in dB, 20 log10 of the ratio). F0-72 measures it from a frequency response.
source: B1 of F0-71 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a steady oscillation whose size is set by a limit in the system, not by how it started.
analogy: the howl that grows until the amplifier is flat out, then stays at that loudness.
precise: an isolated periodic solution of a nonlinear system; in a loop that is linearly unstable, saturation can stop the growth and produce one.
source: B1 of F0-71 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); R3 of F0-71 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how a system answers steady sine waves of different frequencies: how much bigger or smaller, and how much later.
analogy: how strongly the floor shakes at each spin speed, and how far its movement lags the drum.
precise: for a stable linear system G(s), a sine input sin(ωt) gives, after the transient has died out, the output |G(jω)|·sin(ωt + ∠G(jω)); the complex function G(jω) of ω is the frequency response.
source: B1 of F0-72 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); R1 of F0-72 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the size ratio between output and input sine, and the delay between them measured in degrees of a cycle.
analogy: how far the floor moves per unit of drum push, and how far behind it is.
precise: |G(jω)| and ∠G(jω) = arg G(jω); a phase of −90° means the output peaks a quarter period after the input.
source: B1 of F0-72 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a logarithmic way to write a gain, so that multiplying gains becomes adding numbers.
analogy: notches on a volume knob.
precise: gain in dB = 20·log10|G|; ×10 is +20 dB, ×2 is about +6 dB, ×1/√2 is about −3 dB.
source: B1 of F0-72 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); D1 of F0-72 (derivation and arithmetic shown in the chapter, recomputed by its lab runs) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two graphs of the frequency response against frequency on a log scale: gain in dB above, phase in degrees below.
analogy: the washing machine's "shake chart" over its whole speed range.
precise: plots of 20 log10|G(jω)| and ∠G(jω) against log ω; for rational G they are close to straight-line asymptotes that change slope at corner frequencies.
source: B1 of F0-72 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); R2 of F0-72 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the frequency where a simple lag stops passing signals unchanged and starts cutting them down.
analogy: the spin speed above which the floor can no longer keep up.
precise: for 1/(τs + 1), ωc = 1/τ, where |G| = 1/√2 (−3 dB) and the phase is −45°; above it the gain falls at 20 dB per decade. It is the cut-off frequency (−3 dB) of HW302.
source: B1 of F0-72 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); R1 of F0-72 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a large response at one frequency, where the system's own bounce and the push keep in step.
analogy: the floor shaking hard at one spin speed.
precise: for an under-damped second-order system with ζ < 1/√2, |G(jω)| has a maximum near ωn; at ω = ωn exactly, |G| = 1/(2ζ) times the static gain and the phase is −90°.
source: B1 of F0-72 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); R2 of F0-72 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how much extra delay, in degrees, a loop could take before it becomes unstable.
analogy: how much later Mira (F0-70) could feel the shower water before her corrections started making things worse.
precise: 180° + ∠L(jωgc), where ωgc is the gain crossover frequency at which |L(jωgc)| = 1.
source: B1 of F0-72 (Karl Johan Åström, Richard M. Murray, "Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers" — title only, not opened); R4 of F0-72 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
